The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighMemoryUsage on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:23:52Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:24:15Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 15 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 16 minutes 52 seconds {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 17 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 15 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-11T01:44:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:24:53Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 40 minutes 53 seconds {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 2 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:26:16Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.2% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 4.0% {errors_at_worst} - which can't be told apart from its normal variation.
Rise above baseline: can't be told apart from its normal variation - the calm before it began was too short to say how high the rate goes on its own.
The series behind the alert, `max(max_over_time(process_resident_memory_bytes[1m])) / max(container_spec_memory_limit_bytes)` - its alert said "Memory usage climbing against the container limit for 15m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 21.637327414937318% {series_before} before it began, 55.58296192553825% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 83.73364056460559% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did and how much longer requests took: say what both meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Requests took longer at p50, the median request: 44.916666666666664 ms {latency_p50_before} before it began, 119.25 ms {latency_p50_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 291 ms {latency_p50_at_worst} at its worst.
Requests took longer at p95, the slowest one request in twenty: 215.53333333333333 ms {latency_p95_before} before it began, 570.675 ms {latency_p95_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 1442 ms {latency_p95_at_worst} at its worst.
Requests took longer at p99, the slowest one request in a hundred: 381.3666666666667 ms {latency_p99_before} before it began, 1014.85 ms {latency_p99_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 2490 ms {latency_p99_at_worst} at its worst.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T02:24:13Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighMemoryUsage on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T02:24:27Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T02:24:27Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T02:24:35Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:23:52 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T02:24:40Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 361 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T02:24:41Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 01:44 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T02:24:41Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T02:24:43Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 01:45 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T02:24:44Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T02:24:44Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T10.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T02:24:44Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 30 {T11.2} minutes before 02:04 {T11.3}
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T02:24:45Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 80 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T02:24:46Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 2 {T13.2} candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T02:24:46Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T02:24:47Z {T15.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T15.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T15.3} hour before 02:24:46 {T15.4}
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T02:24:51Z {T16.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T02:24:52Z {T17.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T02:24:53Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Restarted io-shop for C1
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T02:25:00Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:25 {T19.2} - up to 126s {T19.3}
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T02:26:15Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:24 {T20.2}
  - [T21] 2026-11-11T02:26:16Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T22] 2026-11-11T02:26:16Z {T22.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - restarted [io-shop] and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T23] 2026-11-11T02:28:03Z {T23.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/531

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 5 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 28 {Gad41.2} minutes, 01:34–02:01 {Gad41.3}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 44 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 30 {G46bc.2} minutes, 01:35–02:04 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 26 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 30 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 01:35–02:04 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 4.00% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 01:53 {Gbac1.7}
  - [G9c6f] WARN io-shop: heap at #MiB of 2048MiB {G9c6f.1} limit - 5 {G9c6f.2} occurrences in 5 {G9c6f.3} minutes, 02:00–02:04 {G9c6f.4}; # was 1033MiB {G9c6f.5} to 1153MiB {G9c6f.6}, typically 1093MiB {G9c6f.7}, highest at 02:04 {G9c6f.8}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Memory in io-shop began climbing on its own at about 2026-11-11T01:41:00Z {C1.1}, from roughly 460MB {C1.2} to 1.8GB {C1.3} against a 2GiB {C1.4} limit, while request volume stayed at 1200 {C1.5}. Latency rose after the heap passed about 1GiB {C1.6}. This is a leak in the running process: nothing was deployed or changed, and the process was never restarted. [resource-leak, confidence 0.8 {C1.7}, confirmed]
  - [C2] Demand saturation is a less likely alternative, because traffic did not rise. [demand-saturation, confidence 0.08 {C2.1}, never tried]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Restarted io-shop for [C1] - confirmed, nothing to put back

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault is in src/io_shop/visits.py. `_LAST_SEEN` is a module-level dict. `record_visit` adds one entry for every new shopper id, and only `forget_every_visit` ever removes anything. The module's own docstring says Io has a few million registered shoppers and that this "holds whichever of them have been by". So a long-running process keeps growing as long as new shoppers keep arriving, even with request volume flat. That fits the incident: memory climbed with steady traffic, no deploy and no restart. tests/io_shop/test_visits.py already describes this ("nothing takes any of it away").
      
      The fix keeps the same API but puts a cap on the store. It is now an `OrderedDict` holding at most `_MOST_SHOPPERS_REMEMBERED` (100,000 {F1.1}) entries. `record_visit` writes the entry and moves it to the newest position. If the store is then over the cap, it drops the oldest entries. A shopper who comes back still costs nothing extra, and recent visitors are still remembered. Losing an entry is harmless because the module already returns `None` for a shopper it doesn't know, which is the normal first-visit path. Updates and evictions happen under a lock, so concurrent renders can't fight over the order. The only caller, `account_page.py`, imports just `record_visit`, and its signature is unchanged.
      
      The new tests check two things. Recording more distinct shoppers than the cap leaves exactly the cap in memory, with the oldest gone and the newest kept. And a shopper who visits again counts as recent, so the next eviction removes someone else. Against the old code, the first test would see the count go past the cap.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:156, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
  - [U2] record_visit at src/io_shop/account_page.py:160, in serve_account_page: calls it: record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Restarted io-shop
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #531 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: In src/io_shop/visits.py, `record_visit`, which serve_account_page calls for each account page it serves, adds an entry for every new shopper id to the module-level dict `_LAST_SEEN`, and nothing in the files Code-Fix read removes entries except `forget_every_visit`. A long-running io-shop process therefore keeps growing in memory as new shoppers arrive, even when request volume stays flat. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: The shop's server likely kept a note of every shopper who visited and never threw any of those notes away, so it used more and more memory the longer it ran.
still_at_risk: As new shoppers visit, memory in the restarted io-shop could climb toward its limit again and slow requests the way it did here.
symptom: Requests to the shop slowed down
causal_chain 1: Requests to io-shop took longer to answer from the onset onward, at the median and even more for the slowest requests. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 2: The io-shop process's memory kept climbing toward its container limit while requests slowed. The application logged a rising heap against its limit, and the growth was confined to the running process: the restart cleared it. (cites AL1; G9c6f, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; M1, under "Actions it took"; T20, under "What Argus did, in order"; T21, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: The memory grew inside the running process with no production change to set it off. No deploy or release was found in the day before the onset, and no flag change in the hour around it. Every replica ran one revision, but the history does not name it, and the record does not show when it went out or show the service healthy after it. That revision was not ruled out. (cites T9, under "What Argus did, in order"; T15, under "What Argus did, in order"; T10, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: Each account page served records the shopper in a store shared across the whole process. According to Code-Fix's reading of visits.py, that store keeps one entry for every new shopper and nothing trims it, so the process grows as new shoppers arrive. (cites U1, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; U2, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus"; F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix")
contributing_factors 1: Only the memory alert found the problem, and its rule waits for its condition to hold before it fires. No alert on io-shop's request latency was seen, even though latency rose from the onset.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on request latency could have flagged the slowdown well before the memory rule's wait ran out, which would have brought the restart sooner and shortened the slow stretch.
contributing_factors 2: No check was seen that catches a process-wide store with no size limit before it ships. The module's own test describes the store growing without anything removing entries, and that was not flagged.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The store would have been bounded before it reached production, and the memory growth behind the slowdown would not have built up.
action_items 1: Add an alert on io-shop's p95 and p99 request latency compared with its usual level, so a slowdown is caught without waiting on the memory rule.
action_items 2: Add a review or lint check to io-shop that flags module-level dicts or caches with no size bound.
action_items 3: Audit io-shop for other module-level stores that add an entry per distinct shopper or user without ever removing any.
action_items 4: Route HighMemoryUsage on io-shop to the on-call paging policy, so a person is paged when it fires.
went_wrong 1: The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
